chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-A'lawi, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said:

I asked him about the mukatab (a slave who has contracted a manumission deed), whether the fitrah of Ramadan is upon him or upon the one who contracted with him, or whether his testimony is valid? He said: 'The fitrah is upon him, and his testimony is not valid.'

key_terms.أَوْ عَلَى مَنْ كَاتَبَهُ: Or upon the one who contracted with him (the master).
key_terms.الْمُكَاتَبِ: A slave who has entered into a contract of manumission (kitabah) with his master.
key_terms.شَهَادَتُهُ: His testimony (as a witness in legal matters).
key_terms.فِطْرَةُ رَمَضَانَ: The specific alms or tax due at the end of Ramadan (Zakat al-Fitr).

ai.seo_question: Is the fitrah of Ramadan the responsibility of the mukatab or his master, and is his testimony valid?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), the legal distinction is made that while the mukatab remains a slave in terms of testimony validity (shahadah), he is fully responsible for his own fitrah of Ramadan, reflecting his partial financial independence. This ruling highlights the nuanced Shia jurisprudence where social and legal status (like the inability to testify in certain contexts) does not automatically negate religious obligations. The hadith underscores the principle that financial capacity, rather than total freedom, determines the burden of specific charitable dues like fitrah.
